body:
Dan Frank's ancestry is a multi-generational blend of Eastern European Jewish (Frank/Harris line from Russia and Austria), Anglo-American Protestant (Gillingham/Lewellen/Van Voorhis), and Appalachian-rooted families centered in southwestern Pennsylvania (Uniontown, Brownsville, Hopwood) and Pittsburgh. Several lines trace back to early 20th-century immigrants — notably [[wiki/people/david-j-frank|David J. Frank]] from Russia and Sadie Harris from Austria — while others reflect long-standing Pennsylvania residents and professionals (e.g., Dr. George Dale Gillingham, DDS).

This hub integrates two independent evidentiary streams:

1. **Documentary genealogy** — an Ancestry.com GEDCOM containing 515 individuals and 218 families, parsed and traced across 7 generations to identify 90 direct ancestors and 16 European-born forebears.
2. **Genomic data** — 23andMe ancestry composition, haplogroup predictions, Neanderthal percentage, health predispositions, carrier status, wellness reports, and trait reports, all extracted from PDF exports.

The two streams corroborate each other at the macro level (21.4% Ashkenazi Jewish matching the known paternal line; 78.3% Northwestern European matching the known maternal lines) while opening specific anomalies that neither stream resolves alone (the maternal R0 haplogroup, the 0.2% Sub-Saharan African trace, the 3.6-point Ashkenazi deficit relative to expectation).

Please see the following pages for detailed records and analysis:
- [[wiki/self/lineage/family-tree]] — Ancestry.com GEDCOM family tree (515 individuals)
- [[wiki/self/lineage/23andme-genomics]] — 23andMe DNA composition, chromosome painting, Neanderthal data
- [[wiki/self/lineage/hybrid-analysis]] — Cross-referenced analysis (speculative)

## Summary of Findings

The 23andMe data and the documentary record confirm each other at the population level. Dan is 99.7% European, with 21.4% Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry matching the known paternal Jewish immigrant line (David J. Frank from Russia, [[wiki/people/sadie-harris|Sadie Harris]] from Austria) and 78.3% Northwestern European matching the known maternal lines (Gillingham, Lewellen, Shrum, Van Voorhis, Coldren, Thomas, Conwell) that have been rooted in Pennsylvania and West Virginia since the 1700s.

Within that broad confirmation, the genomic data introduces anomalies the paper trail cannot explain: a maternal mitochondrial haplogroup (R0) that is unusual for an ostensibly purely Appalachian Protestant line, a paternal Y-DNA haplogroup (R-Z93) more common in Central/South Asia than typical Ashkenazi populations, and a 0.2% Sub-Saharan African trace that has no documentary counterpart. The genomic data also refines what the paper trail suggests: the 21.4% Ashkenazi figure is slightly below the ~25% expected from one fully-Jewish grandparent, a variance that is within normal DNA recombination range but that could also indicate mixed ancestry in the Frank line or a non-paternity event.

## The Four Grandparental Lines

### Paternal Grandfather: Morley Jay Frank (1927–1998)

The Ashkenazi Jewish immigrant line. Morley's parents — David J. Frank (b. 1892, Russia; d. 1960, Brownsville, PA) and Sadie Harris (b. 1900, Austria; d. 1997, Hopwood, PA) — represent the classic pogrom-era flight from Eastern Europe. But the family did not flee directly into the Appalachian coal patch. A direct read of the GEDCOM places David J. Frank in Manhattan in 1900, 1905, and 1910 and in the Bronx in June 1915, reaching Brownsville only by the 1920 census. The immigration terminated in New York City, and the family moved to Fayette County fifteen years later, as a second and separate decision.

[[wiki/people/morley-frank|Morley Jay Frank]] was born in Brownsville, Pennsylvania, served in the military (enlisted 24 October 1945 in Pittsburgh), lived briefly in Seattle in 1957, and then collapsed back to Uniontown/Hopwood/Champion for the rest of his life. He died 13 December 1998 in Hopwood and is buried there. His migration arc — brief westward eruption followed by permanent return to the Fayette County gravity well — is the template Dan's own Full Sail → NYC → return-to-Uniontown arc repeats twice over (2013, then definitively February 2025).

The Frank patrilineal line extends to Henry Frank (b. abt 1815, Germany; d. 1901, Manhattan) and Dorothea Christiana Charlotta Francken (b. 1781), placing the family's German roots five generations back. Henry Frank's residence history — New York City from at least 1843 through 1901 — establishes the Frank family as early Ashkenazi immigrants who arrived in the pre-Civil War wave rather than the later 1880–1920 wave.

### Paternal Grandmother: Gay Gillingham (b. 1939)

The Fayette County Protestant establishment. Gay Gillingham is the daughter of Dr. George Dale Gillingham, DDS (abt 1894–1987) and Frances "Fran" Gillingham, maiden name Lewellen (abt 1903–1956). The Gillingham and Lewellen families are deeply entrenched in Fayette County (Uniontown, North Union) and surrounding counties for generations, dating to at least the mid-1800s. Dr. George Dale Gillingham achieved a level of professional middle-class status as a dentist — a point of modest upward mobility within the regional hierarchy. The family geography is overwhelmingly static and centered around Uniontown, with Dr. Gillingham's death in Florida reflecting a common retirement migration.

The Lewellen line extends to Edward Franklin Lewellen (1862–1954), born in MT Morris, Greene County, Pennsylvania, and Lillie Diwins (abt 1871). The Gillingham line extends to David Gillingham and beyond to William Preston Gillingham (1796, Buckingham, Bucks, PA) and Euphemia Clauson — early colonial settler stock.

Gay Gillingham's own geographic history is minimal: born in North Union, Fayette County, lived briefly in Seattle in 1957 (following Morley), then returned to Fayette County permanently. She represents the stable, territorially-rooted side of Dan's inheritance — the line that never left.

### Maternal Grandfather: George Dixon Shrum Jr. (b. abt 1937)

The Pittsburgh Corridor industrialists. George Dixon Shrum Jr. was born in Pittsburgh, Allegheny County, and his family's history is tied to the orbit of Pittsburgh rather than the deep rural Appalachian lines. His father, G. Dixon Shrum (abt 1896–1960), was born in Irwin, Westmoreland County, served in the military (1917–1918), and moved through North Huntingdon before settling in Pittsburgh's Fox Chapel neighborhood. The family represents the industrial and suburban development around Pittsburgh — working-to-middle-class participants in the 20th-century industrial economy.

The Shrum line extends through Daniel E. Shrum Jr. (abt 1846) and Reuben Shrum (1818) to the early 19th-century settlers of Westmoreland County. The Dixon line (Ida M. Dixon, b. abt 1860) and the Kutz line (Linus Belus Cubulus Kutz, b. 1875, Bowers Station, Pennsylvania) add German and Scots-Irish components. The Kutz and Rush families (Anne Lois Rush, b. 1875, Lower Turkeyfoot, Somerset County) extend into the rural Somerset County region.

Daniel E. Shrum Jr. and Ida M. Dixon married in 1875 and had at least six children, of whom G. Dixon Shrum (abt 1896–1960) is the direct line. One of his older brothers, **Daniel Shrum** (b. 11 April 1884, Pennsylvania), was still single and living at home per the 1900 census (Irwin Ward 2, Westmoreland County) and died 11 December 1918 in Greensburg, Westmoreland County, at age 34 — a death date that falls inside the second, deadliest wave of the 1918 influenza pandemic in Pennsylvania (which peaked in the state that October–December), though the GEDCOM carries no attached cause of death and this reading is inference, not documentation. He never appears elsewhere in the corpus; this is a collateral relative (a great-granduncle, 0% DNA contribution) rather than a direct ancestor, and the fact is recorded here as exactly the kind of mundane, previously-unmined GEDCOM detail `EXTRACTION_SPEC.md` argues is worth keeping even when nothing else connects to it yet.

George Dixon Shrum Jr.'s own life traces a Fox Chapel → Pittsburgh trajectory, with documented residence at multiple Pittsburgh addresses from 1940 through 2020. He married [[wiki/people/diane-moore|Rebecca Diane Van Voorhis]] Jr. in 1961, linking the Pittsburgh industrial line to the Appalachian coal-country line.

### Maternal Grandmother: Rebecca Diane Van Voorhis Jr. (b. 1939)

The Appalachian chaos engine. Rebecca Diane Van Voorhis Jr. ("Diane," also known as Dian Shrum) is the line's one documented departure from the Pennsylvania/West Virginia region — she lived in Farmington Hills, Michigan, from 1985 to 2010, and in Stanwood, Michigan, from 2013 to 2020. She was born in West Virginia and represents the most fragmented, chaotic, and geographically dispersed of the four grandparental lines.

Her mother, [[wiki/people/fran-coldren|Jesse Frances Thomas]] Whyel Coldren (1920–2018), is a nexus of genealogical complexity. Born Jesse Frances Thomas in Fort Martin, West Virginia, she married three times (Whyel, then Coldren, then back to Van Voorhis via her daughter's marriage), carrying a shifting name structure that points to a life marked by multiple marriages and likely significant hardship. Her trajectory — Adkin, McDowell County, WV → Cass, Monongalia County, WV → Smithfield, Fayette County, PA → Miami Beach, FL → Uniontown, PA — is the most geographically mobile of any ancestor in the tree.

The Thomas family (Marion Edward Thomas Sr., b. 1877; Robert M. Thomas, b. abt 1851; Hezekiah Thomas, b. abt 1807) has deep, multi-generational roots in Monongalia County, West Virginia, representing a core Appalachian identity. The Conwell line (Ida Ellen Conwell, b. 1880, WV; Thomas P. Conwell, b. abt 1844) and the Zearly line (Susan A. Zearly, b. 1845, WV) are similarly rooted in the West Virginia coal country.

The Van Voorhis line in this context is verifiably an Appalachian one, rooted in places like Dilliner and Dunkard, Greene County, Pennsylvania. George E. Van Voorhis (b. abt 1889) and his wife Gala Von GAPEN (b. 1892) lived their entire documented lives in Dunkard Township before retiring to St. Petersburg/Gulfport, Florida. The Gapen family (Wilson Lewis Gapen, b. 1852; Haddie E. Gapen, b. 1857) has been in Greene County since at least the 1850s.

This entire quadrant is defined by movement, name changes, and resilience in the face of what was likely significant poverty and social instability. It is the source of Dan's documented dissociative coping mechanisms, comfort with chaos, high tolerance for instability, and deep, almost cellular understanding of survivalism and emotional fragmentation.

## Migration Corridors

Six distinct migration corridors are documented in the ancestry:

1. **Russia → Manhattan (1900) → Bronx (1915) → Brownsville, PA (1920)** — David J. Frank's path: immigration → NYC → Fayette County. The family lived in Manhattan for at least 20 years before moving to Pennsylvania.

2. **Austria → Brownsville, PA (by 1920)** — Sadie Harris's path: apparently direct to Fayette County, though her father "Harris" is listed as born in Czechoslovakia, suggesting the family may have been displaced within Eastern Europe before immigration.

3. **Germany → Manhattan (1815+) → died Manhattan 1901** — Henry Frank's path: early Ashkenazi immigrant (pre-Civil War wave), lived in New York City for over 50 years, died there. His son Max Frank (b. abt 1860, NY) continued the NYC residency through at least 1940.

4. **Scotland → PA/WV (1700s–1800s)** — Andrew Jenkins (b. 1818, Larbert, Stirling, Scotland), Robert Turley (b. abt 1839, Scotland), Rachael Jenkins (b. abt 1842, Scotland), and Jane Hunter (b. abt 1821, Scotland) represent the Scotch Presbyterian and Scots-Irish immigrant wave that settled heavily in southwestern Pennsylvania and West Virginia.

5. **Germany/Palatinate → PA (1700s–1800s)** — The Klein, Krehbiel, and Emerick families represent the German Palantine wave. Susannah Elizabeth Emerick (b. 1848, Allegheny County) and the Krehbiel/Klein clusters reflect this migration. The Emerick line includes John Andrew Emerick and Johann Nicholas Emerick from the German Palatine wave.

6. **Netherlands → Oyster Bay, NY → PA (1600s–1700s)** — The Van Voorhis name is associated with Dutch colonial settlers from Oyster Bay, Long Island. In this tree, the Van Voorhis line is verifiably Appalachian (rooted in Greene and Fayette Counties, PA), but the name carries the colonial Dutch legacy.

## Jewish-Line Ancestry

The Jewish line comprises 19 individuals with Frank, Harris, Cohen, Kutz, Rush, or Dixon surnames. Of these, 4 are direct ancestors who contribute to Dan's DNA:

| Name | Birth | Death | Relationship |

| David J Frank | 12 Aug 1892, Russia | 06 Apr 1960, Brownsville | Great-grandfather (gen 3) |
| Sadie Harris | 14 Dec 1900, Austria | 27 Nov 1997, Hopwood | Great-grandmother (gen 3) |
| Morley Jay Frank | 20 Aug 1927, Brownsville | 13 Dec 1998, Hopwood | Grandfather (gen 2) |
| Richard Harrison Frank | 22 May 1959 | — | Father (gen 1) |

Collateral Jewish-line relatives (siblings, cousins, spouses — 0% DNA contribution but relevant for family structure) include Meyer Cohen (Germany), Bertha Cohen (Germany), Hannah Frank (Gunzenhausen, Germany), Carrie Frank (NYC), Max Frank (NYC), Henry Frank (Germany), and Harris (Czechoslovakia — Sadie's father, the only documented paternal-line Jewish ancestor beyond Sadie herself).

The Kutz, Rush, and Dixon surnames appear on the **maternal** side (Shrum line), not the Jewish paternal side. Their inclusion in the Jewish-line list is based on surname association only — they may or may not be Jewish. Linus Belus Cubulus Kutz (b. 1875, Bowers Station, PA) married Erma K. Shrum, connecting the Kutz name to the maternal Shrum line.

### The Harris Paternal Line Gap

The most significant data gap in the Jewish line is the complete absence of documentation beyond Sadie Harris herself. Her father is listed only as "Harris" from Czechoslovakia. No given name, no birth date, no immigration record, no residence history. This man contributed ~12.5% of Dan's DNA (one great-grandparent) but is completely undocumented beyond a single datum.

## Cross-Referencing with 23andMe

The 23andMe data and the documentary record confirm each other at the macro level while opening specific anomalies:

| Metric | Expected from GEDCOM | Actual from 23andMe | Variance |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ashkenazi Jewish | ~25% (one fully-Jewish grandparent) | 21.4% | -3.6% |
| British & Irish | ~30% (maternal Gillingham/Lewellen/Shrum lines) | 55.8% | +25.8% |
| French & German | ~30% (maternal Shrum/Van Voorhis/Coldren lines) | 22.2% | -7.8% |
| Sub-Saharan African | 0% | 0.2% | +0.2% |

### Reconciling the Variances

The British & Irish overperformance and French & German underperformance likely reflects the reality that 23andMe's reference panels classify most of the German and Pennsylvania Dutch ancestry as "British & Irish" rather than "French & German." The German settlers of southwestern Pennsylvania intermarried heavily with British colonists, and their DNA is often indistinguishable from the British & Irish reference population.

The Ashkenazi deficit of 3.6 percentage points is within normal DNA recombination variance (a grandparent typically contributes 18–32% of DNA) but could also indicate that Morley Jay Frank was not 100% Ashkenazi — that one of his parents had mixed ancestry. This is consistent with the possibility that Sadie Harris's father ("Harris" from Czechoslovakia) may have been partially non-Jewish (Czech rather than Jewish), or that David J. Frank's line included a non-Jewish ancestor.

The 0.2% Sub-Saharan African trace has no documentary counterpart and may represent statistical noise at the detection threshold, or it may indicate a single ancestor 7–8 generations back on any line.

## Haplogroup Analysis

### Maternal Haplogroup: R0

R0 is the ancestral haplogroup of H and V, the most common mitochondrial haplogroups in Europe. R0 itself is relatively rare in Northern Europe and is found at higher frequencies in the Arabian Peninsula, the Middle East, and among some Ashkenazi Jewish populations.

On the maternal line (Suzanne → Diane → Fran → Ida Ellen Conwell → Susan A. Zearly → Amelia), this is unexpected for a supposedly purely Appalachian Protestant lineage. Possible explanations include:

1. **Distant Jewish or Middle Eastern ancestor** on the maternal line, possibly entering through the Van Voorhis Dutch colonial line or the Conwell/Thomas Appalachian line.
2. **R0 was more common in ancient Europe** than currently recognized, and the maternal line preserves an ancient European variant.
3. **Undocumented adoption or non-paternity event** on the maternal line within the last few generations.

### Paternal Haplogroup: R-Z93

R-Z93 is a subclade of R1a, found in Central/South Asia and some Ashkenazi Jewish populations (particularly the Levite lineage). This is consistent with the Frank line's Ashkenazi heritage, though R-Z93 is not the most common Ashkenazi Y-DNA haplogroup (which would be J1, J2, E1b1b, or R1b).

Possible explanations:

1. **R-Z93 is found in some Ashkenazi populations**, particularly associated with the Levite lineage and other groups with Central Asian connections.
2. **The Frank line may have Central Asian or Eastern European roots** that predate the Ashkenazi bottleneck.
3. **Non-paternity event** in the Frank line — a non-Jewish ancestor entering the line within the last few generations.

## Notable Ancestors

### David J. Frank (1892–1960)

The patriarch. Born in Russia (12 August 1892), immigrated to the United States and settled in Manhattan by 1900. Naturalized in 1929 in Chicago, Illinois. Lived in Manhattan through at least 1915 (Bronx), then moved to Brownsville, Fayette County, Pennsylvania, by 1920. Died 6 April 1960 in Brownsville. Buried in Hopwood, Pennsylvania.

His geographic trajectory — Russia → Manhattan → Bronx → Brownsville — is the family's foundational migration story. He represents the Ashkenazi Jewish immigrant experience: fleeing the collapsing empires and pogroms of Eastern Europe, spending a generation in New York City, then moving to the industrial coal towns of Pennsylvania as a second and separate decision.

### Sadie Harris (1900–1997)

The matriarch. Born in Austria (14 December 1900), she appears in the 1920 census in Brownsville, Fayette County, Pennsylvania, and remained there through at least 1993. Died 27 November 1997. Buried in Hopwood, Pennsylvania.

Her 97-year lifespan — from the Austro-Hungarian Empire to the 21st-century United States — is the family's longest documented tenure in a single location. She never left Fayette County after arriving, and her burial in Hopwood (the same cemetery as David J. Frank, Morley Jay Frank, and Fran Coldren) resolves the family's terminus to that specific place.

### Morley Jay Frank (1927–1998)

The geographic template. Born in Brownsville, Pennsylvania (20 August 1927), served in the military (enlisted 24 October 1945), lived briefly in Seattle (1957), then returned to Uniontown/Hopwood/Champion for the rest of his life. Died 13 December 1998 in Hopwood. Buried there.

His migration arc — brief westward eruption followed by permanent return to the Fayette County gravity well — is the template Dan's own Full Sail → NYC → return-to-Uniontown arc repeats twice over (2013, then definitively February 2025). The pattern is documented across four generations of the paternal line.

### Fran Coldren (1920–2018)

The matriarchal fracture point. Born Jesse Frances Thomas in Fort Martin, West Virginia (15 August 1920), she married three times (Whyel, then Coldren, then back to Van Voorhis via her daughter's marriage). Her shifting name structure — Jesse Frances Thomas Whyel Coldren — encodes a life of reinvention and survival through multiple partnerships.

Her geographic trajectory — Adkin, McDowell County, WV → Cass, Monongalia County, WV → Smithfield, Fayette County, PA → Miami Beach, FL → Uniontown, PA — is the most mobile of any ancestor. She died 4 April 2018 in Uniontown, Pennsylvania.

### Jesse Frances Thomas Whyel Coldren

The archetype of emotional dissociation via reinvention. Fran's great-grandmother (Ida Ellen Conwell, b. 1880, WV; Susan A. Zearly, b. 1845, WV; Amelia, b. abt 1813, WV) represents the deep Appalachian matrilineal line that the ancestral-dialectic frame reads as the source of Dan's dissociative coping mechanisms.

## Gaps and Unresolved Questions

1. **The Harris paternal line.** Sadie Harris's father ("Harris" from Czechoslovakia) is the single biggest data gap. He contributed ~12.5% of Dan's DNA but is completely undocumented beyond a single datum. Research into Czech immigration records, census data, and synagogue records could resolve this.

2. **The maternal R0 haplogroup.** The origin of the R0 mitochondrial haplogroup on the maternal line is unexplained. It may indicate a distant Jewish, Middle Eastern, or Central Asian ancestor entering through the Van Voorhis, Conwell, or Thomas lines. Research into the specific maternal-line ancestors (Conwell, Zearly, Amelia) and their origins could resolve this.

3. **The paternal R-Z93 haplogroup.** The R-Z93 Y-DNA haplogroup is consistent with Ashkenazi heritage but is not the most common Ashkenazi haplogroup. Determining whether this represents the Levite lineage, a non-paternity event, or Central Asian ancestry requires further investigation.

4. **The 0.2% Sub-Saharan African trace.** This may be statistical noise or may indicate a real ancestor 7–8 generations back. Checking chromosome location and segment size could determine whether this is a real signal.

5. **Henry Frank and Hannah Frank's relationship.** The GEDCOM shows Henry Frank (b. Germany, abt 1815) and Hannah Frank (b. Gunzenhausen, 1818) as Max Frank's parents or as his father and his father's second wife. Clarifying this relationship determines whether Hannah Frank is Dan's direct ancestor (~6.25% DNA) or a collateral relative (0% DNA).

6. **The Cohen connection.** Meyer Cohen and Bertha Cohen (both born in Germany) appear in the GEDCOM as siblings or spouses of direct ancestors. Clarifying their relationship to the Frank/Harris line would determine whether they contribute to Dan's DNA.

7. **The Dixon and Kutz lines.** Ida M. Dixon (b. abt 1860, PA) and Linus Belus Cubulus Kutz (b. 1875, Bowers Station, PA) appear on the maternal Shrum line. Their surnames suggest Scots-Irish and German ancestry, but their specific origins are undocumented beyond the GEDCOM.

8. **Place name inconsistencies.** The GEDCOM contains numerous place name variants ("Pennslyvania," "Westmorland Co," "Fayette" vs "Fayette County" vs "Fayette, Pennsylvania") that complicate geographic analysis. Standardizing these names would improve data quality.

9. **The Lincoln line.** 31 individuals with the Lincoln surname appear in the GEDCOM. Their relationship to the direct ancestry is unclear — they may be a collateral line or may indicate a distant connection to the Lincoln family name (though not necessarily to Abraham Lincoln himself).

10. **Incomplete health report extraction.** Two 23andMe health predisposition results (Age-Related Macular Degeneration, Hereditary Thrombophilia) were not fully extracted from the PDF. The Prostate Cancer (BRCA1/BRCA2) report is locked behind an incomplete questionnaire.

gaps.text: 2. **The maternal R0 haplogroup.** The origin of the R0 mitochondrial haplogroup on the maternal line is unexplained. It may indicate a distant Jewish, Middle Eastern, or Central Asian ancestor entering through the Van Voorhis, Conwell, or Thomas lines. Research into the specific maternal-line ancestors (Conwell, Zearly, Amelia) and their origins could resolve this.

gaps.text: 3. **The paternal R-Z93 haplogroup.** The R-Z93 Y-DNA haplogroup is consistent with Ashkenazi heritage but is not the most common Ashkenazi haplogroup. Determining whether this represents the Levite lineage, a non-paternity event, or Central Asian ancestry requires further investigation.

gaps.text: 4. **The 0.2% Sub-Saharan African trace.** This may be statistical noise or may indicate a real ancestor 7–8 generations back. Checking chromosome location and segment size could determine whether this is a real signal.

gaps.text: 5. **Henry Frank and Hannah Frank's relationship.** The GEDCOM shows Henry Frank (b. Germany, abt 1815) and Hannah Frank (b. Gunzenhausen, 1818) as Max Frank's parents or as his father and his father's second wife. Clarifying this relationship determines whether Hannah Frank is Dan's direct ancestor (~6.25% DNA) or a collateral relative (0% DNA).

gaps.text: 6. **The Cohen connection.** Meyer Cohen and Bertha Cohen (both born in Germany) appear in the GEDCOM as siblings or spouses of direct ancestors. Clarifying their relationship to the Frank/Harris line would determine whether they contribute to Dan's DNA.

gaps.text: 7. **The Dixon and Kutz lines.** Ida M. Dixon (b. abt 1860, PA) and Linus Belus Cubulus Kutz (b. 1875, Bowers Station, PA) appear on the maternal Shrum line. Their surnames suggest Scots-Irish and German ancestry, but their specific origins are undocumented beyond the GEDCOM.

gaps.text: 8. **Place name inconsistencies.** The GEDCOM contains numerous place name variants ("Pennslyvania," "Westmorland Co," "Fayette" vs "Fayette County" vs "Fayette, Pennsylvania") that complicate geographic analysis. Standardizing these names would improve data quality.

gaps.text: 9. **The Lincoln line.** 31 individuals with the Lincoln surname appear in the GEDCOM. Their relationship to the direct ancestry is unclear — they may be a collateral line or may indicate a distant connection to the Lincoln family name (though not necessarily to Abraham Lincoln himself).

gaps.text: 10. **Incomplete health report extraction.** Two 23andMe health predisposition results (Age-Related Macular Degeneration, Hereditary Thrombophilia) were not fully extracted from the PDF. The Prostate Cancer (BRCA1/BRCA2) report is locked behind an incomplete questionnaire.
